title: Recursion Fundamentals
tagline: Base case, recursive case, and the call-stack mental model that unlocks trees, graphs, and DP.
intro:
Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It feels like magic until you internalise one idea: **trust the recursion**. Assume the recursive call already returns the correct answer for the smaller input, then just combine it with the current step. Stop trying to trace every call in your head — that way lies madness.

Recursion is the gateway to half of this curriculum. Trees, graphs, backtracking, divide-and-conquer, and top-down DP are all recursion with extra structure. If recursion is shaky, those topics feel impossible; once it clicks, they feel obvious.

This module nails the two-part anatomy (base case + recursive case), the call-stack model that explains *why* recursion works and when it overflows, how to read a recurrence's complexity, and when to convert recursion to iteration.
objectives: Write any recursion as a base case plus a recursive case that shrinks the input
Use the call-stack model to predict execution order and stack depth
Distinguish head recursion (work after the call) from tail recursion (work before)
Derive recursion complexity with the branches^depth rule and recurrence relations
Recognise when recursion overflows the stack and convert it to iteration
Apply the divide-and-conquer template (split, solve halves, combine)

signals: The problem is defined in terms of itself (tree node = value + subtrees)
"Generate all ..." subsets / permutations / combinations → backtracking recursion
Divide the input in half and combine (merge sort, binary search)
Structure is nested or hierarchical (trees, nested lists, file systems)
antiSignals: Simple linear iteration is clearer (don't recurse to sum an array)
Recursion depth could exceed ~10^4–10^5 → risk of stack overflow, prefer iteration
Overlapping subproblems with no memo → exponential blowup, add DP

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Recursion is solving a big problem by trusting a smaller copy of yourself to handle the smaller version - like Russian nesting dolls. You open a doll, find a smaller identical doll inside, and keep going until the tiniest one that doesn't open (the base case). Then everything closes back up.

The secret is to stop tracing every call in your head and simply trust the smaller answer. Example: `factorial(3)` means '3 times whatever factorial(2) gives me'. You trust factorial(2) hands back 2, so factorial(3) becomes 6. Each call quietly waits on a smaller one until factorial(1) = 1 starts the chain coming back.

sections.heading: The anatomy of every recursion
sections.body:
Every correct recursion has exactly two parts. Miss either and it breaks.

| Part | Job | Failure mode if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Base case** | The smallest input you answer *directly*, no recursion. | Missing → infinite recursion → stack overflow |
| **Recursive case** | Solve a *smaller* input, then combine with the current step. | Doesn't shrink → never reaches base case |

The golden rule: **every recursive call must move strictly closer to a base case.** If the input doesn't get smaller (shorter array, fewer nodes, smaller number), the recursion never terminates.

sections.heading: The call-stack mental model
sections.body:
Each call pushes a **frame** onto the call stack holding its local variables and where to resume. When a call returns, its frame pops and control returns to the caller. The base case is what lets the stack start unwinding.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["factorial(3)"] --> B["factorial(2)"]
  B --> C["factorial(1) = 1 (base)"]
  C -. returns 1 .-> B
  B -. returns 2*1=2 .-> A
  A -. returns 3*2=6 .-> R["result 6"]
```

The calls go **down** to the base case, then results bubble **back up**. The maximum number of frames alive at once is the **recursion depth** — and that is your space cost. Too deep and you get a `StackOverflowError` / `RecursionError`.

callouts.text: Default stack depth is ~10^4 in Python and ~10^4–10^5 in the JVM. A recursion that goes n deep on n = 10^6 will overflow — convert it to an explicit stack or a loop.

sections.heading: Head vs tail recursion
sections.body:
The distinction is *where the work happens relative to the recursive call*.

- **Tail recursion**: the recursive call is the last action; nothing happens after it returns. Some languages optimise this into a loop (no stack growth) — but **Java and Python do NOT**, so it still costs O(depth) stack.
- **Head recursion**: work happens *after* the recursive call returns (like `n * factorial(n-1)`). This is the common case and inherently needs the stack to remember the pending work.

Knowing the difference matters because tail-recursive shapes are the easiest to rewrite as clean iterative loops when you need to kill the stack cost.

sections.heading: Complexity of recursion
sections.body:
Two tools cover almost everything.

**1. The branches^depth shortcut.** Count how many recursive calls each call makes (branches) and how deep the tree goes (depth). Total calls ≈ branches^depth.

**2. Recurrence relations** for divide-and-conquer, via the Master Theorem intuition:

| Recurrence | Example | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) | factorial, linear recursion | O(n) |
| T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) | binary search | O(log n) |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) | merge sort | O(n log n) |
| T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) | naive Fibonacci, subsets | O(2^n) |

Space is the **maximum depth** of the recursion (longest root-to-base path), because that's how many frames coexist.

callouts.text: Naive Fibonacci is O(2^n) because it re-solves the same subproblems. Add a memo (cache) and it drops to O(n) — that single change is the bridge from recursion to dynamic programming.

sections.heading: The divide-and-conquer template
sections.body: A huge family of efficient algorithms follows one shape: **split the input, solve each half recursively, combine the results.** Merge sort, quicksort, and many tree algorithms are instances.

codeExamples.label: Merge sort — divide and conquer
codeExamples.code:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:                 # base case
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left = merge_sort(a[:mid])      # solve half
    right = merge_sort(a[mid:])     # solve half
    return merge(left, right)       # combine

def merge(l, r):
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(l) and j < len(r):
        if l[i] <= r[j]: out.append(l[i]); i += 1
        else: out.append(r[j]); j += 1
    return out + l[i:] + r[j:]

sections.heading: When (and how) to convert to iteration
sections.body:
Convert recursion to iteration when depth could overflow the stack, or when an explicit loop is simply clearer. The mechanical conversion: replace the call stack with your own explicit **stack** (a list/deque), pushing the state you'd otherwise pass to the recursive call.

Linear tail-style recursions (factorial, list traversal) become simple `for`/`while` loops. Tree/graph DFS becomes a `while stack:` loop that pops a node and pushes its children. BFS uses a **queue** instead of a stack to get level-order instead of depth-first.

interviewTalking: When you choose recursion, say it explicitly: "This problem is self-similar — each subtree is the same shape — so I'll solve it recursively. My base case is an empty node returning 0; the recursive case combines the answers from the left and right subtrees." Always state the base case first; it proves you won't infinite-loop. Then give the complexity using branches^depth or the recurrence, and flag the stack depth as your space cost.
commonMistakes: Missing or wrong base case → infinite recursion and stack overflow
Recursive call that doesn't shrink the input → never terminates
Forgetting recursion depth is O(depth) space (the call stack)
Re-solving overlapping subproblems without memoisation → exponential time
Assuming Java/Python optimise tail calls — they don't; deep tail recursion still overflows
Mutating shared state across calls without undoing it (a backtracking bug)
complexityNotes: Recursion time is (branches per call)^(depth) for branching recursion, or solved via the recurrence T(n) for divide-and-conquer. Space is the maximum recursion depth (frames alive simultaneously): O(log n) for balanced splits, O(n) for linear or skewed recursion.
